title: The Ermine With the Thaw
creature: An ermine who carries the thaw in her mouth
summary: She will not put it down until somebody in the valley asks her to, properly.

chapters.title: What She Carries
chapters.text: The ermine came down the scree in November and went up again in March and in between she was somewhere on the mountain with her mouth full. Everybody in the valley had seen her at least once. She was not shy and she was not hiding; she went along the top of the dry-stone walls in broad daylight with the confidence of something that has never been caught. In summer she was brown with a white front. From the first snow she was white all over except the tip of the tail, which stayed black, and which was the only part of her you could actually see against a drift — a small black comma travelling along a wall at speed with nothing attached to it. And from November she carried the thaw. You could see it if she stopped, which she did about once a minute, sitting up on her back legs the way they do to look at you. There was something in her jaws. It was not large — the size of a hen's egg, perhaps — and it was not any colour, which is the difficulty; Lise had looked at it four times at close range over three winters and could only ever say that it was the same colour as the day after tomorrow. It was warm. You could tell from a distance of two metres. On the coldest morning of the year, standing at the wall with the frost cracking in the grass, you could feel it on your face like an open oven door, coming off a thing the size of an egg being carried by an animal that weighed less than a cup of coffee. Lise had tried, once, at nine, to work out how she could carry something that warm in her mouth all winter without it doing her any harm, and had been told by her father to stop asking questions of that kind about that particular animal. She had not stopped. She had simply stopped asking him. She would not put it down. That was the whole of the arrangement and everybody in the valley knew it. She would carry it all winter, up and down the scree, through the snow and under it, without ever setting it down for a second — not to eat, not to sleep, not for anything — until somebody came up and asked her, properly, to let it go. And then it would be spring. Not in a week. Not gradually. There were photographs in the parish office, four of them, taken by a man called Anton in the 1960s who had been a serious person about photography: the same view of the same slope on four consecutive days, and on the third one there is snow to the wall-top and on the fourth one there is grass, and everybody who sees them for the first time says the same thing, which is that the man had obviously cheated. He had not cheated. The four negatives are in the same strip, in order, with the frame numbers on them, and they have been looked at by two people from a university who came up in 2003 and were extremely polite and went away again. What happens is not that the snow melts. Melting takes days and leaves the ground wet and the drifts hollowed out and grey at the edges, and everybody in that valley has watched melting happen every spring of their lives and knows exactly what it looks like. The snow goes. There is no water. That is the part that nobody from outside believes and that nobody inside bothers arguing about. The ground under it is dry.

chapters.title: The Asking
chapters.text: Nikolai Braun had done the asking for forty-one years and he was not going to be doing it a forty-second. He had had a stroke in the September. He was alive and he was at home and he was, by all accounts, entirely himself in the head, and he could not walk to the end of the lane, let alone up the scree. The valley discussed the problem for most of October in the way that valley discussed everything, which was by not discussing it in front of children and then discussing it at length in front of children who were pretending to read. Lise, who was twelve, learned the following. That the asking was not a ceremony. There were no words. Nobody wore anything. If you went up there expecting to say a formula, Nikolai had told the last three people who asked him, you would come down again with nothing having happened and you would feel extremely silly. That you went alone, and in the last week of February or the first of March, and you went up to wherever she was, and you asked, and either she put it down or she did not. That it had not always been Nikolai. Before him it had been a woman called Frau Ebner for a very long time, and before her a man whose name was on the war memorial, and before that the records got vague. And that in 1934, and again in 1968, the person who went up had come back down without it, and both of those springs had come in the second week of May and both of those years had been hard. 1968 was in living memory when Lise was small. Frau Hofer, who was ninety and who had been a young woman that year, would talk about it if you got her going: the hay running out in March, the road shut until the twenty-first of April, the two families who left the valley that summer and did not come back. She never once said who had gone up that year and failed, and nobody else ever said it either, and Lise worked out at about ten that this was deliberate and that the name was known to everyone over sixty. What nobody could tell Lise, because nobody knew, was what *properly* meant. She asked her mother, who said she supposed it meant being sincere. She asked Herr Vogel at the shop, who said it meant you had to mean it, which was the same answer with fewer syllables. She asked Nikolai Braun himself, in the front room of his house, in November, with his daughter listening from the kitchen and pretending not to. He took a long time to get the sentence out. That was one of the things the stroke had left him. He said: "It means you have to know what you're asking for." Lise said that everybody knew what they were asking for. They were asking for spring. And Nikolai Braun laughed, which was alarming, and then took another long time, and said: "That's what I said in 1962. And I came down that day and it was still there in her mouth and I was up that mountain three more times before the ninth of March."

chapters.title: The First Time
chapters.text: She went up on the twenty-sixth of February. It had been agreed, in the way things were agreed there — which is to say that nobody had ever said to Lise *you are doing it*, and yet by the end of January there was no other candidate and everyone had stopped mentioning alternatives. She was not the obvious person. She was twelve. But the valley had seven households left in it and four of those were people over seventy, and of the rest there was Lise, her brother who was six, and the Marek boys who were nineteen and twenty-two and who had both said no in a way that closed the subject. It took her two hours and forty minutes to get up to the shoulder, in good weather, with a flask. Her father walked with her as far as the second gate, which was as far as anybody was allowed to come, and stood there while she went on up. She did not look back until the bend, and when she did he was still there, and she was extremely annoyed with herself for looking. Above the second gate the path stops being a path. It is a line of slightly-less-bad ground across a slope of loose grey stone, and in February it has snow on it in the hollows and ice under the snow, and Lise went up it in her brother's crampons, which were too big, taking the long zigzag her father had made her promise to take. The ermine was on the wall by the ruined byre, which is where Nikolai had said she would be, and she sat up when Lise came round the corner and looked at her with the egg-sized nothing glowing in her jaws. Lise had thought about it for four months and had prepared nothing, on purpose, because everyone had told her that preparing was the mistake. She said: "Please can you put it down." Nothing happened. She said it again, and then she said it a third time in dialect rather than in school German, in case that was the thing. The ermine sat on the wall and looked at her and did not put it down. Lise stayed up there for about an hour. She sat on the wall herself, at a distance, and she talked. She said all the reasonable things: that the valley needed the grass, that the Hofers had run out of hay, that her father's back would not stand another month of it. She said, at one point, feeling humiliated, that she was sorry she was not Nikolai. The ermine washed her face with one front paw, which is a thing they can do while holding something, and which Lise found extremely rude. Then she went along the wall and off into the rocks. Lise came down the mountain in the dark, badly, having stayed too long, and was met halfway by her father with a torch who did not ask her anything at all until they were inside. When they were inside, and she had her boots off, he asked her whether she was cold, and she said no, and he said good, and that was the entire conversation about it. She heard him on the telephone to Nikolai's daughter later, through the floor, saying it had not worked, in a voice that was not disappointed at all — and she lay in bed working out that he had never expected it to, and that he had not said so, and that both of those had probably been kindnesses.

chapters.title: What Properly Means
chapters.text: She went up twice more in the following week and got nothing, and on the third of March she went to see Nikolai Braun and told him she was finished. She said it in a temper. She said that she had asked, and had meant it, and that if he had a magic word he ought to hand it over, and that she was not going up there again to be looked at. Nikolai listened all the way through. His daughter brought coffee and left. Then he said, in his slow way, with a great many pauses: "What do you want the spring for." Lise said, for the grass. He shook his head, slightly. She said, for the hay, for the Hofers, for the road. He shook his head again and did not say anything, and the silence went on long enough to be a question. And Lise sat in that front room in a bad temper and heard herself say something she had not known she was going to say, which was: "Because I can't do another one." Nikolai did not move. "I can't do another winter here," she said. "There's seven houses and my brother's six and there's nobody. I've got two more years of the bus and then I'm going to Innsbruck and I'm not coming back, and everybody knows it and nobody will say it, and I'm going to be the one who leaves and Papa is going to be here on his own with the wall." She stopped. "That's what I want the spring for," she said. "I want it to be March so it's April so it's June so I can get out." There was a very long pause. "Yes," said Nikolai Braun. "That's it. That's the asking." She went up on the fifth. She found the ermine on the same wall. She did not make a speech. She sat down about three metres away with her hands in her sleeves and she said the true thing, out loud, in the cold, to a weasel. The ermine listened — she is prepared to be argued with about the word *listened* and will not move on it — and then came four metres along the wall towards her, which she had never done, and opened her mouth, and put it down in the snow. Then she went off into the rocks with her tail up. The snow was gone from the lower slope on the eighth. Lise has the date because she wrote it in the back of a school exercise book, next to a sum she had got wrong. She did go to Innsbruck, at eighteen, and she did not come back, in the sense that she does not live there. She goes up every February. She has done it for nineteen years. She takes the train and then the bus and then she walks, and she asks, and it has worked every time, and the true thing she says has been different every single year.
